name: Esomeprazole
route_note: Oral delayed-release capsules, tablets or granules once daily; IV injection or infusion

discovery.note: Single S-enantiomer of omeprazole, which is metabolised more slowly by CYP2C19 and gives higher exposure. Year of the patent; approved in 2000.

rx_status: prescription; OTC for heartburn in many countries
tagline: S-enantiomer of omeprazole, the 'purple pill' for acid reflux
summary: Esomeprazole is the S-isomer of omeprazole and works the same way, irreversibly inhibiting the gastric proton pump. Marketed as Nexium, it became one of the best-selling drugs of the 2000s and is often cited as an example of a chiral switch.
mechanism: Like omeprazole, esomeprazole is activated in the acidic parietal-cell canaliculus to a sulfenamide that covalently binds the H+/K+ ATPase, blocking the final step of acid secretion.
The S-enantiomer is less dependent on CYP2C19 for clearance than the R-enantiomer, giving higher and less variable plasma exposure at a given dose.
uses: Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease and erosive oesophagitis
Prevention of rebleeding after endoscopic treatment of peptic ulcers (IV)

history.title: First approval
history.detail: Nexium is approved in Sweden and then in the EU.

history.title: US approval
history.detail: FDA approves Nexium in February as Prilosec's patent nears expiry.

history.title: OTC
history.detail: Nexium 24HR is approved for over-the-counter use in the US.

history.title: US generics
history.detail: Generic esomeprazole becomes available in the US.

facts: Nexium's launch is frequently cited as an example of 'evergreening' through a single-enantiomer switch.
Esomeprazole is combined with naproxen in Vimovo to reduce NSAID ulcer risk.

references.title: AstraZeneca – Nexium receives fast first approval in Sweden (2000)
